section_summary: This section documents growing U.S. and Allied concern over exports to Japan of petroleum products, scrap iron, steel, bearings, aircraft-related goods, and strategic minerals such as copper, tungsten, tin, antimony, cobalt, and molybdenum. It includes public and congressional protests, State Department explanations of export controls, reports on Japanese purchasing in China and South America, and successful diplomatic efforts to prevent Dominican scrap-iron shipments. A substantial group of duplicated enclosures discusses Mauricio Hochschild’s mineral sales, followed by a La Paz despatch disputing his account of tungsten transactions involving Japan and Germany.

subfiles.title: L. R. Johnson letter forwarding a clipping about tank plate for Japan
subfiles.about: Johnson forwards a seemingly authentic report of tank-plate exports to Japan and calls it an inconsistency in American policy.
subfiles.summary: L. R. Johnson forwards a sensational but apparently authentic clipping about tank plate for Japan and hopes the senator's health improves.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Senator Bone on exports of tank plate
subfiles.about: The Department answers Senator Bone’s inquiry about tank-plate exports to Japan by supplying export-control regulations and policy statements.
subfiles.summary: Hull acknowledges Bone’s February 11 letter and the enclosed January 22 letter from L. R. Johnson. He supplies regulations, press releases, and a proclamation issued under the Export Control Act, emphasizing that licenses outside the British Empire and Western Hemisphere depend on national-defense needs. Johnson’s letter is returned.

subfiles.title: Fragment of London telegram no. 536 on British oil and raw-material exports
subfiles.about: The telegram reports British statements on oil supplies to Japan and export controls throughout the British Empire.
subfiles.summary: London telegram 536 fragment: British oil contracts with Japan, no British legal obstacle to US oil purchases except aviation grades; Lord Cecil says exports are licensed and nickel and copper sometimes barred; consultation continues.

subfiles.title: Tientsin telegram on large Japanese gasoline inquiries
subfiles.about: Caldwell reports Japanese inquiries for unusually large gasoline supplies for North China.
subfiles.summary: Tientsin: Standard Vacuum was asked via Mitsui for 5.6 million gallons of gasoline for North China Communications; a Mitsubishi order reportedly sought 18.5 million more, driven by fears of frozen credits and an embargo.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Hercules Powder Company pine-oil sales to Japan
subfiles.about: Yost records David Houston’s warning about rapidly increasing Japanese purchases of scarce American pine oil.
subfiles.summary: Japan's Hercules pine-oil purchases rose from 70,000 to about 330,000 gallons in 1940; pine oil is a flotation reagent; Houston warns restricting it could shift demand to Shell's cresylic acid.

subfiles.title: Representative Ford letter transmitting a petroleum-coke complaint
subfiles.about: Ford forwards William R. Harriman’s letter and a Los Angeles Times clipping concerning petroleum-coke sales to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Representative Ford transmits Harriman's petroleum-coke complaint and a newspaper article for consideration.

subfiles.title: William R. Harriman letter on a petroleum-coke clipping
subfiles.about: Harriman sends Ford a Los Angeles Times clipping about petroleum-coke sales to Japan and suggests possible action.
subfiles.summary: Harriman notes later rules may have addressed the issue but finds the October 27, 1940 article worth Ford's attention.

subfiles.title: Hull reply to Representative Ford on petroleum-coke exports
subfiles.about: Hull says petroleum-coke exports and related issues are under interagency consideration.
subfiles.summary: Hull says the Department and other agencies are considering petroleum coke and related products, and returns Harriman's letter.

subfiles.title: Senator Wiley letter enclosing an Auburn clipping on suspicious shipments
subfiles.about: Wiley sends Hull a newspaper item alleging suspicious westbound shipments of TNT, rails, and tank plate.
subfiles.summary: Senator Wiley encloses an Auburn clipping on TNT, rail and tank-plate shipments believed destined overseas.

subfiles.title: State Department reply on licensing controlled exports
subfiles.about: Hull explains the Department’s licensing policy for strategic exports in response to the suspicious-shipment clipping.
subfiles.summary: Hull: licenses generally issued for the British Empire and Western Hemisphere when surpluses allow; aviation gasoline and scrap barred elsewhere; other goods licensed sparingly.

subfiles.title: Representative Hendricks letter forwarding a constituent appeal
subfiles.about: Hendricks forwards a Florida correspondent’s letter and resolution concerning exports and asks for consideration.
subfiles.summary: Representative Hendricks transmits a constituent's appeal and resolution; much illegible.

subfiles.title: Hull reply to Representative Hendricks regarding further restrictions
subfiles.about: Hull states that additional export restrictions are under continuing interagency consideration and returns the constituent materials.
subfiles.summary: The surviving portion says that the question of further restrictions was receiving constant and careful consideration by all interested government agencies. Miss Barto’s letter and enclosure were returned. The listed informational enclosures included the National Defense Act, proclamations, executive materials, and a resolution.

subfiles.title: Ciudad Trujillo telegram reporting scrap iron intended for Japan
subfiles.from: G. Howland Shaw Scotten, Ciudad Trujillo
subfiles.about: Scotten asks whether he should approach the Dominican government about 1,000 tons of scrap iron reportedly awaiting shipment to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Ciudad Trujillo: a Japanese steamer expected around March 6 for about 1,000 tons of scrap; Scotten asks instructions on approaching Dominican authorities.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on the Dominican prohibition of scrap-iron exports
subfiles.about: The memorandum reports that Dominican customs had barred scrap-iron exports without prior Treasury authorization.
subfiles.summary: Dominican customs circular of February 25 ordered no scrap-iron exports without Treasury approval, following the Legation's exchanges on a Japan shipment.

subfiles.title: Dominican customs circular prohibiting unauthorized scrap-iron exports
subfiles.about: The circular orders Dominican customs offices to prevent scrap-iron exports unless previously authorized by the Treasury and Commerce Secretariat.
subfiles.summary: Dominican Circular Letter 463 requires customs staff to enforce the ban on unauthorized old-iron exports.

subfiles.title: Instruction to Ciudad Trujillo concerning Cuban general export licenses
subfiles.about: The instruction transmits information about U.S. general export licenses for Cuba and rules governing reexports.
subfiles.summary: Specified controlled articles could be exported to Cuba under general licenses, while other controlled goods still required individual licenses. The Department was considering comparable general licenses for additional Western Hemisphere countries. The first page is heavily corrupted by OCR.

subfiles.title: Telegram directing an informal approach to the Dominican government
subfiles.about: Hull instructs the Legation to seek Dominican cooperation in preventing scrap-iron exports outside the Western Hemisphere.
subfiles.summary: Hull instructs the Legation to explain confidentially that the US, Colombia, Cuba, Mexico and others restricted scrap exports outside the hemisphere, hoping the Dominicans follow.

subfiles.title: Under Secretary’s note recommending a Dominican approach
subfiles.about: Welles recommends a confidential explanation of U.S. scrap-iron policy to the Dominican government.
subfiles.summary: Welles favors informing the Dominican government of the US position and Mexico's precedent unless Hamilton objects.

subfiles.title: New Sing appeal for stronger restrictions on Japan
subfiles.about: Sing urges the United States to stop supplying Japan with war materials and asks why stronger action has not been taken.
subfiles.summary: Chinese students' spokesman Sing says Chinese resistance matters to American security, and asks about Japan's purchases, the lack of embargo action, and supplies to an Axis member.

subfiles.title: Hamilton reply to New Sing on export controls
subfiles.about: Hamilton acknowledges Sing’s appeal and supplies laws and regulations governing exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton encloses the Defense Act, proclamations and regulations; aviation gasoline, lubricating oil and scrap are restricted, other goods variably controlled.

subfiles.title: Commerce Department inquiry about discarded rails
subfiles.about: Wythe requests specifications and location information needed to assess possible American interest in discarded rails.
subfiles.summary: Commerce says the Iron and Steel Scrap Institute expects interest in the rails but doubts a trip is justified without details on condition, weight and location.

subfiles.title: British Embassy letter on a cobalt shipment aboard SS Imperial
subfiles.about: Dent reports Chilean action that may prevent a cobalt shipment to Japan aboard the SS Imperial.
subfiles.summary: British Embassy: Chile's Caja de Crédito Minero refused the cobalt deal; Dent welcomes likely prevention of the Japanese shipment and notes the cobalt was already aboard in New York, needing no license.

subfiles.title: Telegram requesting investigation of 4,000 tons of Dominican scrap
subfiles.from: Sumner Welles, Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Welles asks the Legation to investigate a reported 4,000-ton scrap shipment to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Harry Harris and Company report Sotomayor has 4,000 tons of Dominican scrap, including 250 tons of nickel-steel armor plate, for a Japanese ship; the Department would not welcome it.

subfiles.title: Scotten telegram promising Dominican cooperation
subfiles.from: G. Howland Shaw Scotten, Ciudad Trujillo
subfiles.about: Scotten reports that the Dominican president promised to prevent scrap-iron shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Scotten raised scrap with the Dominican president, who promised full cooperation and immediate action to stop scrap going to Japan.

subfiles.title: John S. Taylor appeal to stop all aid to Japan
subfiles.about: Taylor urges Bryson to introduce legislation ending American exports and assistance to Japan.
subfiles.summary: John Taylor finds it astonishing the US supplies Japan with scrap and gasoline while aiding China, and urges Bryson to sponsor a complete cutoff.

subfiles.title: Hull letter returning the Taylor correspondence to Bryson
subfiles.about: Hull acknowledges Bryson’s transmittal of Taylor’s protest and encloses a copy of the Department’s reply.
subfiles.summary: Hull returns Taylor's February 21 letter to Bryson, with a copy of the reply to Taylor.

subfiles.title: Hochschild report on South American mineral exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Hochschild surveys Japanese purchases of strategic minerals from Chile, Bolivia, Peru, and Argentina and proposes measures to redirect the trade.
subfiles.summary: Hochschild says Japan buys Chilean, Bolivian, Peruvian and Argentine metals on price and textile countertrade; ending it needs South American cooperation and long-term US purchasing at stable prices.

subfiles.title: Feis acknowledgment to Schubart concerning Hochschild’s report
subfiles.about: Feis thanks Schubart for the Hochschild report and circulates it within the Department.
subfiles.summary: Feis acknowledges Schubart's note and Hochschild photostat, passing them to interested offices.

subfiles.title: Instruction forwarding the Hochschild papers to Santiago
subfiles.about: The Department sends the Schubart and Hochschild correspondence to the Embassy in Santiago for information.
subfiles.summary: Instruction to Santiago forwarding Schubart's January 28 letter and Hochschild's January 27 report on mineral exports to Japan.

subfiles.title: Schubart cover letter concerning accusations against Hochschild
subfiles.about: Schubart forwards Hochschild’s explanation of his companies’ ore sales to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Schubart says Hochschild was accused of unpatriotic tungsten sales but gave satisfactory explanations; sends a photostat for verification.

subfiles.title: Hochschild mineral-export report enclosed for Santiago
subfiles.about: This enclosure details mineral exports from four South American countries to Japan and recommends a coordinated purchasing alternative.
subfiles.summary: Hochschild report: Japanese price premiums and cheap textiles draw copper, molybdenum, antimony, tin, tungsten and lead; stable long-term US purchases and government cooperation proposed.

subfiles.title: Instruction forwarding the Hochschild papers to La Paz
subfiles.about: The Department sends the Schubart and Hochschild correspondence to the Legation in Bolivia.
subfiles.summary: Instruction to La Paz forwarding the Schubart letter and Hochschild report on mineral exports to Japan.

subfiles.title: Schubart cover letter enclosed for La Paz
subfiles.about: Schubart explains why he is providing Hochschild’s account of South American ore sales to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Schubart's cover letter for La Paz: Hochschild's tungsten sales were called unpatriotic, his explanations satisfactory; verification invited.

subfiles.title: Hochschild mineral-export report enclosed for La Paz
subfiles.about: The report surveys Japanese mineral procurement across South America, with particular attention to Bolivian wolframite.
subfiles.summary: Hochschild says small and medium Bolivian producers favored Japan’s higher tungsten prices and that the Banco Minero would handle the trade even if his firm withdrew. He offers similar accounts of Chilean, Peruvian, and Argentine exports. He recommends coordinated government action and guaranteed U.S. purchases to replace Japanese demand.

subfiles.title: Instruction forwarding the Hochschild papers to Lima
subfiles.about: The Department forwards the Schubart and Hochschild correspondence to the Embassy in Peru.
subfiles.summary: Instruction to Lima forwarding the Schubart letter and Hochschild report on strategic mineral exports to Japan.

subfiles.title: Schubart cover letter enclosed for Lima
subfiles.about: Schubart forwards Hochschild’s defense of his South American companies’ sales to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Schubart's cover letter for Lima: recurring allegations about Hochschild's tungsten sales, explanations satisfactory, government check invited, cooperation offered.

subfiles.title: Hochschild mineral-export report enclosed for Lima
subfiles.about: The enclosure describes Japanese purchases of South American strategic minerals and suggests replacing them with stable American demand.
subfiles.summary: Hochschild report for Lima: Japan's better prices and textile trade draw Chilean, Bolivian, Peruvian and Argentine ores; an embargo needs producer governments' cooperation and long-term US contracts.

subfiles.title: Instruction forwarding the Hochschild papers to Buenos Aires
subfiles.about: The Department sends the Schubart and Hochschild correspondence to the Embassy in Argentina.
subfiles.summary: Instruction to Buenos Aires forwarding Schubart's cover letter and Hochschild's report on mineral exports to Japan.

subfiles.title: Schubart cover letter enclosed for Buenos Aires
subfiles.about: Schubart submits Hochschild’s account of ore sales to Japan for government examination.
subfiles.summary: Schubart's cover letter for Buenos Aires: rumors of unpatriotic tungsten trading; satisfied by explanations but sends the report for verification.

subfiles.title: Hochschild mineral-export report enclosed for Buenos Aires
subfiles.about: The report describes Japanese mineral purchases in South America and proposes economic measures to curtail them.
subfiles.summary: Hochschild report for Buenos Aires: Japanese prices and textile countertrade draw metals away; producing governments need incentives; proposes diplomatic cooperation and fixed-price long-term US purchasing.

subfiles.title: Feis memorandum to Welles on the Hochschild communication
subfiles.about: Feis calls Welles’s attention to Hochschild’s letter amid discussions of South American strategic-material sales to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Feis tells Welles the Bank of Manhattan communication and Hochschild's letter bear on current policy about South American sales of strategic materials to Japan.

subfiles.title: Immigration Section general-card-index search sheet
subfiles.from: Division of Communication and Records, Immigration Section
subfiles.about: The sheet records a search for file numbers under an alien’s name, but no usable name or entries appear in the OCR.
subfiles.summary: Only the printed form headings are legible. The page does not preserve an identifiable person’s name or any file-number results.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on alleged Mexican concessions to Japanese interests
subfiles.about: The memorandum flags a New York Times article about concessions allegedly granted by Mexican official Modesto C. Rolland.
subfiles.summary: Memo on allegations that Rolland favored Japanese interests in Mexico and promised concessions to American promoters, including a manganese option; ending incomplete.

subfiles.title: New York Times clipping, “Mexico Opens Inquiry”
subfiles.about: The clipping reports a Mexican investigation into alleged maladministration benefiting Japanese commercial interests.
subfiles.summary: New York Times clipping: Mexico's attorney general opened an inquiry into former under secretary Modesto Rolland, linked to an oil concession for a Japanese-controlled company and an import permit.

subfiles.title: Robinson letter on petroleum export-control definitions
subfiles.about: Robinson recommends wording and technical thresholds for controlling crude oils and aviation lubricants.
subfiles.summary: Robinson and Dr. Wilson reject "economically feasible commercial processes" as too subjective, recommend "commercial distillation" and a viscosity-index threshold of 65, and note steam-refined aviation lubricant stocks were already covered.

subfiles.title: Senator Wiley letter concerning alleged Ford aircraft bombing Canton
subfiles.about: Wiley asks Hamilton to comment on a clergyman’s allegation that Ford-built aircraft had bombed Canton.
subfiles.summary: Senator Wiley forwards Reverend Edwin Kennedy's protest over alleged Ford aircraft bombing Canton and asks a duplicate reply.

subfiles.title: Kennedy protest over alleged American-made bombers in Canton
subfiles.about: Kennedy protests reports that aircraft bearing Henry Ford’s name were used to bomb Canton.
subfiles.summary: Kennedy says friends returned from China were bombed in Canton by planes marked with Ford's name, and asks Wiley to stop war-supply sales to Japan.

subfiles.title: Hull reply on aircraft exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Hull responds that no aircraft were exported to Japan in 1940 and only one in 1939 under U.S. export licenses.
subfiles.summary: Hull encloses a February 18 press release listing arms and war-supply exports during 1940. He adds that Ford had produced only a few planes in 1932 before discontinuing aircraft operations, making current bombing by Ford-built planes highly unlikely unless the aircraft were very old. Kennedy’s letter is returned.

subfiles.title: Timken renewed inquiry about bearing exports to Japan and Russia
subfiles.from: W. E. Umstattd, Timken Roller Bearing Company
subfiles.about: Timken seeks an unofficial policy judgment before fulfilling substantial Japanese bearing orders.
subfiles.summary: Timken has $270,000 in Japanese bearing orders for March to May and $75,000 in new inquiries; its president renews a request for guidance on exports to Japan and Russia.

subfiles.title: Timken’s original inquiry on sales to Japan and Russia
subfiles.about: Timken asks whether continued acceptance of Japanese and Russian bearing orders accords with government policy.
subfiles.summary: Timken's original inquiry: bearing exports to Japan and Russia were negligible but rising as supplies shift from Germany and Sweden; it seeks guidance to avoid acting against policy.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to O. J. Cannon on scrap-iron licenses
subfiles.about: The Department denies that scrap-iron export licenses were issued for Japan and asks Cannon to identify the ships he observed.
subfiles.summary: Reply to O. J. Cannon: scrap can be licensed only for the Western Hemisphere and Britain under the September 26, 1940 policy; asks ship names and destinations.

subfiles.title: La Paz despatch challenging Hochschild’s account of tungsten sales
subfiles.from: Allan Dawson, American Legation, La Paz
subfiles.about: Dawson disputes Hochschild’s claim that a British blockade expert encouraged continued tungsten sales to Japan.
subfiles.summary: La Paz despatch: Royden sought to stop Japanese acquisition of Bolivian tungsten and antimony; Hochschild allegedly sold tungsten to Banco Minero for export to Japan; Dawson agrees stable long-term US contracts could help.

subfiles.title: Singapore telegram on Malayan tin and rubber controls
subfiles.about: Patton reports that Malaya would maintain stringent limits on tin and rubber exports to Japan to prevent indirect supply to Germany.
subfiles.summary: Singapore: the colonial secretary told Japan's consul general that assurances against reexport to Germany would not suffice, as Japan could reexport Thai or Indochinese imports; more Japanese buying elsewhere means cuts in Malayan quotas.

subfiles.title: Congressional referral slip transmitting an enclosure to the State Department
subfiles.about: An unidentified congressional office refers an enclosed communication to the State Department for consideration and a report.
subfiles.summary: Congressional referral slip asking favorable consideration and a report; subject and sender illegible.
